title: Rotary Vane Compressor

introduction.definition: A rotary vane compressor has an off-centre slotted rotor inside a cylinder. Vanes slide out against the cylinder wall and trap air in cells that grow on the inlet side and shrink on the outlet side, compressing the air. Oil injected into the cells seals and cools.
applications: Vacuum/pressure duty in packaging and printing
key_points: Oil-flooded designs reach ~ 7–10 bar in one stage
introduction.summary: A rotary vane compressor has a slotted rotor turning off-centre in a cylinder. Vanes slide out against the cylinder wall and divide the space into cells. On one side the cells grow and draw air in; on the other side they shrink and compress the air before it leaves through the discharge port. Oil injected into the cells seals and cools.

foundation: Mount on a rigid, level foundation or grouted baseplate sized for the machine mass and dynamic loads (typically ≥3–5 × machine mass for reciprocating machines).
Check for soft foot before final bolting.
alignment: Align driver and driven shafts with a laser or dial-indicator method to the coupling maker's tolerances; re-check hot alignment where thermal growth is significant.
piping: Support suction and discharge piping independently so no pipe strain reaches the casing; fit flexible connections where vibration or thermal movement is expected.
Install inlet filters/strainers and isolation valves; add drains and vents.
commissioning: Check rotation direction with the coupling disconnected.
Fill lubricant to the correct level and grade.
Start unloaded where possible; record vibration, temperatures, current and pressures as a baseline.

routine.task: Check oil level and discharge temperature.

periodic.task: Change oil, filters and separator element.

overhaul.task: Check vane height and stator bore; replace vanes.

lubrication: Compressor oil injected into the cells; same oil lubricates bearings.

video_tutorials.title: Rotary Vane Compressor — Introduction

script.narration: This module introduces the Rotary Vane Compressor.
A rotary vane compressor has an off-centre slotted rotor inside a cylinder.
Vanes slide out against the cylinder wall and trap air in cells that grow on the inlet side and shrink on the outlet side, compressing the air.
Oil injected into the cells seals and cools.
Typical applications include workshop and small industrial air; vehicle-mounted compressors; vacuum/pressure duty in packaging and printing; gas boosting at low ratio.
The cutaway reveals the internal construction: Compressor Stator (Cylinder) with Ports, Slotted Rotor & Shaft (eccentric), Vane 1, Vane 2.
The exploded view separates every component so each one can be tapped for its function, material and failure modes.
Next, watch the operation tutorial to see how it works.

script.narration: How the Rotary Vane Compressor works.
The rotor turns off-centre in the stator; vanes slide out by centrifugal force to touch the wall.
On the inlet side, cells between vanes grow and draw air in.
Further round, the cells shrink and the air is compressed.
Compressed air leaves through the discharge port to the oil separator.
The flow overlay traces the liquid from suction to discharge.

video_tutorials.title: Rotary Vane Compressor — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Rotary Vane Compressor.
Check oil level and discharge temperature.
Change oil, filters and separator element.
Check vane height and stator bore; replace vanes.
Watch for capacity loss: lower pressure/flow. Common cause: worn vanes, stuck vanes (varnish).
Watch for overheating: high-temperature trip. Common cause: low oil, dirty cooler.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.

questions.question: What makes the vanes touch the stator wall?
questions.explanation: They slide out in the slots.

questions.question: Why must the rotor be off-centre?
options: So the cell volume changes as it turns
questions.explanation: Eccentricity makes cells grow and shrink.

questions.question: Vane wear is "self-compensating" because…
questions.explanation: They move out to keep contact.
